title: Ecosystem services enhanced through soundscape management link people and wildlife
setting: recreation (Muir Woods National Monument, California; 559-acre old-growth coast redwood forest trail system, ~0.6 km main-trail segment with 19 mitigation signs; >1 million visitors per year)
design: field-experiment (non-randomised paired week-on/week-off signage manipulation over 10 weekly blocks, 14 March-22 May 2016; continuous acoustic recording, calibrated trail counters, walking-speed timing and visitor-intercept survey)
sample_n: 537 survey respondents (55% response; analytic subsets 240 / 434-453 / 453-535); 1,932 timed walking-speed observations (958 sign absent, 974 sign present); acoustic unit: 13 ARUs, 14,040 measured hours (792 site-days in Wilcoxon test; 3,650 hourly observations from 5 counter-ARU pairs in GAM)
exposure: Reverse: educational A-frame signs (e.g. 'Enter Quietly') asking visitors to speak softly, mute phones/electronics and have children walk quietly, placed in alternating weekly blocks (existing quiet signage covered in sign-absent weeks); hourly visitor counts from calibrated trail counters. Acoustic outcome: hourly and daily-averaged background L50 dB(A) from 13 Roland R-05 acoustic recording units 2-250 m from the trails (05:00-21:00). Soundscape perception outcomes: self-reported ability to hear natural sounds, perceived number of bird types, and 6-point soundscape pleasantness (the latter modelled on hourly L50).
behaviour_measure: Visitor walking speed (m/s) timed between visual markers on 9 trail walkways (23.6-59.1 m); hourly visitor count on the trail (log10, calibrated counters) as the crowd/visitation predictor of sound level; the sign-prompted quiet behaviour itself (voice level, electronics use) was not directly measured
measurement_method: observation (stopwatch timing of identified visitors between markers); sensor-GPS-video (calibrated trail counters for visitor counts); self-report (on-site visitor-intercept tablet survey for soundscape perception)
key_finding: Quiet-behaviour signage lowered daily-averaged L50 from 40.8 to 39.6 dB(A) (-1.19 dB(A)), and sound level rose more slowly with visitor numbers when signs were present (500 visitors: 44.0 vs 38.4 dB(A)), an acoustic equivalent of a 20.6% reduction in visitation. Walking speed did not differ between sign-absent and sign-present blocks (1.03 vs 1.01 m/s). Reported ability to hear natural sounds did not differ by treatment, but visitors perceived more bird diversity under mitigation and higher hourly L50 lowered the probability of a 'very pleasant' soundscape rating.
effect_stats: §3.1: daily L50 signs absent 40.8 ± 0.13 vs present 39.6 ± 0.12 dB(A) (mean ± SE), Wilcoxon rank-sum n = 792, W = 85,337, p = 0.016; GAM n = 3,650: log10Visitor Count β = 2.39, F = 880.7, df = 1, p < 0.001; s(Hour, df = 4) β = -0.14, F = 103.8, df = 1, p < 0.001; Treatment β = -0.49, F = 19.1, df = 1, p < 0.001 (Figure 2a). §3.3: walking speed 1.03 ± 0.02 vs 1.01 ± 0.02 m/s, Kruskal-Wallis χ2 = 3.2, df = 1, p = 0.08; ability to hear natural sounds by treatment β = -0.08 ± 0.16, p > 0.05, 95% CI -0.3 to 0.22 (Table 2, n = 199 vs 254); perceived bird types treatment × species β = 0.30 ± 0.14, p = 0.03, 95% CI 0.03-0.60 (n = 240); pleasantness ~ hourly L50 β = -0.18 ± 0.07, p = 0.01, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.04 (n = 453).
